description: We are a team passionate about making NASA’s Earth science accessible through sound. Our name says it all: we convert Earth’s visual stories into real-time sonifications — turning EIC frames into an “Earth Jukebox” that you can hear.
summary:
The planet has always been making music. We just made it playable.

EarthSight2Sound turns NASA Earth imagery into music anyone can play. A user uploads a satellite image with a short description. Within seconds, our pipeline converts it into a 20–30 second audio track using a patched version of the open-source image2sound library, which maps pixel colour to musical pitch. The image and its soundscape are then published to a public feed where anyone can browse and listen.

The challenge asks for a way to experience Earth Information Center visuals through sound, so that blind and low-vision people and the wider public can engage with Earth science. Our app makes this a shared, living jukebox rather than a one-off demo. It is built with accessibility first: one audio player, full keyboard control, ARIA sliders and a text description for every track. Sound lets people feel patterns in a changing planet, such as glowing night lights, smoke plumes and ocean currents, that they might otherwise miss.
details:
What it does and how it works

Users upload a PNG, JPEG or WebP (up to 10 MB) with a description. The backend validates it in layers: client-side Zod, then a head_object check on size and MIME type before any bytes are downloaded, then a 50-megapixel decompression-bomb guard, then the shared description schema. Each failure returns a specific status (413, 415 or 422). A first-in-first-out job queue (one job at a time) runs the pipeline. It resizes the image to 512 px (JPEG q85), runs image2sound, and fits the WAV to a size budget by stepping the sample rate down about 15% per pass without changing the duration. It then uploads the image and audio to Cloudflare R2 and writes a feed row to MariaDB. The frontend polls the job every 2 s and redirects to the refreshed feed. Temp files are always cleaned up, and orphaned audio is deleted on failure.

About image2sound

It is an open-source Python utility by jaerrib on Codeberg. It converts each pixel’s RGB values to a frequency, then shapes them using musical key, tempo, time signature, waveform and ADSR envelopes. These envelopes remove the clicks that older versions produced. Its “reveal” mode derives key and tempo from the image itself. It also has a MIDI composition engine and a CMYK “quartet mode” that maps colours to violin, viola and cello. We vendored it and extended it with --min-duration and --max-duration, duration clamping (trim or loop), 16 kHz 16-bit mono output, and ID3 cover art, so that it works as a reliable web service component.

Benefits

Gives blind and low-vision users a way into EIC visuals.

Needs nothing installed and has no login.

Everything is public, so the collection grows with each upload.

Deterministic output: the same image always gives the same sound.

Intended impact

The aim is to widen who can engage with NASA Earth science, and to become a shared, ever-growing “playlist of the planet” that educators, museums and accessibility advocates can use.

Tools and technology

TypeScript, Python 3.11, Bun, Hono, Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19, Tailwind 4, Zod, Drizzle ORM, MariaDB, Cloudflare R2 (S3 API), sharp, pnpm workspaces, Bun test, Testing Library, Playwright, and image2sound.

Creativity

We turned sonification into a social platform instead of a one-off converter. Adding a public feed turns each image into a track that people can listen to, discover and share. Technically, structural guarantees (one audio element, ports and adapters) replace conventions that are easy to break.

Factors we considered

Accessibility: keyboard operation, ARIA roles, and descriptions for every track.

Safety: layered validation, bomb guard and size limits.

Reliability: guaranteed cleanup, no orphaned files, and a single queue store.

Cost and size: byte-budget fitting keeps audio light for slow connections.

Musicality: envelopes, scales and tempo, to avoid raw-pixel noise.

Honesty: image2sound maps colour to pitch artistically. It is not a calibrated data measurement, and we say so.
